glossary_blurbs.definition: The great Jewish temple in Jerusalem — Solomon's original, rebuilt as the Second Temple — and the spiritual center of ancient Judaism. The Romans destroyed it in 70 CE, which is why Julian's attempt to rebuild it would have undercut a Christian prophecy.

The bishop of Rome and head of the western (Latin) church — and, after Pepin's donation, a territorial ruler in central Italy as well. The papacy's drift away from the Byzantine emperor toward the Franks is a running thread in this chapter.

The bishop of Rome and head of the Latin church. Innocent III had called the Fourth Crusade and explicitly forbade attacking Christian cities — which is exactly what the crusaders did, first at Zara, then at Constantinople.

The bishop of Rome, who had brokered the Union of Florence and organized the failed crusade of Varna. By 1453 the western powers, the papacy included, were too preoccupied to send Constantinople any real aid.
Of greater Iran — the Persian-speaking cultural sphere whose architecture, court ceremony and bureaucratic vocabulary the Sultanate inherited through its Ghaznavid and Ghurid predecessors.

Of the Himalayas, the high mountain range walling off the northern edge of the Indian subcontinent — here the foothills where the fugitive Khwarazmian prince Jalaluddin disappeared after escaping Genghis Khan at the Indus.
Of Pakistan, the modern state carved from northwestern British India in 1947, which today claims the Koh-i-Noor alongside India and Afghanistan as a contested colonial-loot trophy.
Of Afghanistan, the mountainous Central Asian country immediately northwest of the Khyber Pass — one of the modern claimants to the Koh-i-Noor, which passed through Afghan hands under the Durranis.
Of Morocco, the far-western Islamic land on the Atlantic edge of North Africa — homeland of the great traveler Ibn Battuta, who served Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a judge for eight years.
Followers of Islam — here the Turkic-Persian ruling minority governing a Hindu-majority population, a defining tension of Sultanate rule.
Of Bengal, the rich rice-growing delta region of eastern India and modern Bangladesh — whose own sultanate patronized a flourishing Bengali-language literature in the fifteenth century.
Shia Muslims from Iran — immigrants who flocked to the Deccan sultanate courts and competed for influence with the local Sunni Turkic and Indian Muslim factions.
Of the Pashtun highlands straddling modern Afghanistan and Pakistan — the warrior background of the Lodi dynasty that would soon take the Delhi throne.
Of greater Iran — the Persian-speaking heartland where Sufism took its classical institutional form before spreading east into Sultanate India.
Of the Arabic-speaking Islamic heartland (Arabia, the Levant, Egypt) — the older centers of Sufi practice against which the more Hindu-open Indian Chishti tradition defined itself.
Of Bengal in eastern India — one of the regional vernaculars into which the originally Tamil Bhakti devotional movement spread during the Sultanate period.
Of Hungary, the central-European kingdom whose army Suleiman the Magnificent shattered at Mohacs in 1526 — the European twin of Babur's gunpowder victory at Panipat the same year.
Of the Pashtun highlands of modern Afghanistan and Pakistan — the homeland of the Lodi dynasty, the last rulers of the Sultanate before Babur.
Followers of Islam — whose geographic distribution across the subcontinent, set during three centuries of Sultanate rule, foreshadowed the religious map of the 1947 Partition.
The Arabian Peninsula — source of the war-horses the Sultanate's perpetually cavalry-short armies imported by sea, and a hub of the Indian Ocean trade network.
Of the Indonesian archipelago (the Spice Islands and Java) — origin of the cloves, nutmeg and pepper that moved through the same Indian Ocean routes the Sultanate's ports tapped.
Of the steppe-and-oasis belt north of Iran (Transoxiana, the Ferghana valley) — the homeland from which both the Sultanate's Turkic founders and its Mughal destroyers under Babur originated.

The caravan trade across the Sahara desert that moved West African gold and salt north to the Mediterranean. In the fourteenth century it was the pipeline feeding Mali's gold into the Egyptian markets that Italian banking houses tracked.

The medieval habit of reworking pagan classical texts to fit Christian meaning — reading Virgil or Ovid as veiled Christian allegory rather than as literature in their own right. The humanists' break was to stop doing this and read the ancients on their own terms.

The caravan trade across the Sahara that carried West African gold north. Its desert routes seem to have been poor plague vectors, which may be why Mali was spared the Black Death that gutted Eurasia.

glossary_blurbs.definition: The Safavid dynasty's forced conversion of Persia to Twelver Shia Islam after 1501, which turned Iran into the great Shia state of the early-modern world — the religious counterweight to the Sunni Ottomans next door.

The Armenian trading diaspora, centered on the Safavid silk hub of New Julfa, that carried Persian silk westward to European markets including Venice — middlemen of one of the period's most lucrative long-distance trades.

The slow-witted defender of the old Earth-centered cosmos in Galileo's Dialogue. The name puns on 'simpleton' — and Pope Urban VIII, recognizing his own arguments in Simplicio's mouth, took it as a deliberate insult.
The Armenian trading diaspora out of the Safavid silk hub of New Julfa, who carried Persian silk to European markets including Venice in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

The English rendering of al-jabr, the Arabic word that gives us 'algebra.' It names a specific move: when an equation has a negative term, you 'restore' it by adding the same positive quantity to both sides until the negative is gone.

Western European Christian warriors of the holy wars launched from 1095 to seize and hold the Holy Land. Their armies and the small states they planted on the eastern Mediterranean coast were a chronic military pressure on the Islamic world for nearly two centuries (told in full in Chapter 9).

Western European Christian holy-warriors of the Levant campaigns (1095 onward). Their leaders and coastal states were a recurring adversary on Islam's Mediterranean frontier — and several of them were among the high-profile targets of the Assassins.
